about_page_description: I build the systems that make sound work.
about_journey_p1: I started with classical piano, but I never liked just performing. I wanted to know *how* sound worked. That curiosity took me from music school to physics and math, then to game audio. Now I don't just design sounds—I write the C++ and Python code to make them work in real-time.
about_journey_p2: I built an ML system that recognizes beatbox in real-time because off-the-shelf tools were too slow. I wrote a Wwise fixer script because I got tired of manually repairing broken references after every Perforce pull. Right now I'm at DAE in Belgium, turning all this into professional game dev skills.
about_drives_p1: I like fixing things. Why are footsteps playing on the wrong surface? Why did we blow the memory budget? In Not Today Darling, I got boost sounds from 160MB to 2MB because four players on one screen doesn't leave much room.
about_drives_p2: I also like making tools. When Wwise kept breaking after Perforce pulls on Shadow Frames, I wrote a script to fix it automatically. Saved the team hours of manual work.
about_dev_ml_desc: Built a beatbox classifier that responds in 45ms
contact_subtitle: I usually reply within a day or two. Happy to talk about game audio, tools, or middleware work.
about_bio: I work with Wwise, C++, and Unreal Engine. In Shadow Frames, footsteps change based on surface type. Enemy proximity shifts the music. That's what I build—audio that reacts to gameplay.
skills_subtitle: Tools I use daily with project examples

tech_fmod_desc: Event-based workflows, parameter control for adaptive audio. Used in Richter for spatial sound design.

philosophy_quote: In Shadow Frames, anomalies must always be audible. If you can't hear one approaching because the ambient's too loud, I broke my own mix.
principle_clarity_desc: What does the player need to hear right now? That's the first question. In Shadow Frames, I duck environment sounds when enemies get close. Info, not noise.
principle_technical_desc: In Not Today Darling, I had 150MB for all audio. Four players, shared screen, no room for waste. You learn limits fast when you hit them.
principle_layering_desc: The creature in Amorak has four layers: lion for the roar, elephant for weight, tiger for aggression, hippo for texture. Each layer can be mixed independently based on what's happening.
principle_collaboration_desc: Shadow Frames is a three-school collab. I work with writers from RITCS and composers from KASK. Good audio needs that back-and-forth—playtests show what works.
